Thursday was the 32nd anniversary of the founding of W3C. @dontcallmeDOM noted: "I'm proud that W3C has been a shepherd of the web and encouraged at all the people at W3C who are passionate about a web designed for the good of its users."

32 is a power of two (2^5), so a nice milestone for the geeks among us. To celebrate our 0b100000th anniversary, we've updated our donation pages to power of 2 values — for donations above 2^32, please DM us.
https://www.w3.org/support-us/donate
#GivingTuesday #SupportW3C

“This is for everyone” or “free-for-all”?

The web has shifted from its original open, sharing-focused vision toward concerns over protecting vulnerable populations, copyright and AI data usage, and centralized social media that obscure data sharing and provenance.

Pierre-Antoine Champin and Viivi Lähteenoja will lead a mini-workshop at TPAC2026 in Dublin to explore new forms of data governance, data ownership, and decentralized alternatives.
https://github.com/w3c/strategy/issues/567
#w3cTPAC #DataGovernance

@jab01701mid @dalias

In the event that is a good faith question, W3C's Vision and Ethical Web Principles both center a web for *humanity*.

If discussions on AI agents on the web are going to happen (and they will), isn't it to be preferred that they happen at a place where our process centers accessibility, security, privacy etc for humans? Specific to ODRL, wouldn't it be good to consider ways to make sure creator and user privacy rights are considered in AI use?

https://www.w3.org/mission/#vision

If discussions on AI agents on the web are going to happen (and they will), isn't it to be preferred that they happen at a place where our process centers accessibility, security, privacy etc for humans? Specific to ODRL, wouldn't it be good to consider ways to make sure creator and user privacy rights are considered in AI use?

We are pleased to announce the report from the W3C Workshop on the Future of ODRL held in July.

There was consensus to establish a new W3C ODRL Working Group set to work on ODRL 3.0 as a foundation for machine-readable, interoperable and increasingly machine-actionable policies, capable of operating across sectors and integrating with complementary standards for identity, provenance, legal information, data spaces and digital contracts.

The Data Shapes Working Group has published a First Public Working Draft of SHACL 1.2 Inference Rules.

This document defines the Inference Rules support of the SHACL Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL). While the Core part of SHACL focuses on the basic syntax of shapes and constraint validation of data graphs, the SHACL Inference Rules cover features that can be used to infer new triples from existing triples in the data graph.
